problem: A $9\,000\,\text{mL}$-capacity tank initially holds $6\,000\,\text{mL}$ of a brine (salt-water) solution containing $180\,\text{g}$ of salt. Fresh water begins to flow into the tank at a rate of $90\,\text{mL/s},$ while the completely mixed brine flows out at a rate of $60\,\text{mL/s}.$ Find the amount of salt in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow.

feedback.problem: A $9\,500\,\text{mL}$-capacity vat initially holds $6\,500\,\text{mL}$ of a sugar-water solution containing $300\,\text{g}$ of sugar. Pure water begins to flow into the vat at a rate of $100\,\text{mL/s},$ while the completely mixed sugar-water flows out at a rate of $80\,\text{mL/s}.$ Find, rounded to two decimal places, the amount of sugar in the vat at the moment it begins to overflow.
feedback.worked_solution:
Let $Q$ be the amount of sugar in the vat at time $t.$ Then, the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in seconds. This is equal to the rate at which sugar enters the vat minus the rate at which sugar leaves the vat.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{g}/\text{s}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which sugar enters the vat.

First, note that pure water (i.e., a solution containing $0\,\text{g/mL}$ of sugar) enters the vat at a rate of $100\,\text{mL/s}.$ So, the rate at which the *sugar* enters the vat is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{mL}})\cdot (100\,\frac{\text{mL}}{\text{s}}) \\  & =(0\,\frac{\text{g}}{\cancel{\text{mL}}})\cdot (100\,\frac{\cancel{\text{mL}}}{\text{s}}) \\  & =0\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{s}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which sugar exits the vat.

To find the rate at which sugar leaves the vat, we must first determine the volume of sugar-water in the vat at time $t.$

The vat initially contains $6\,500\,\text{mL}$ of solution; pure water enters at $100\,\text{mL/s},$ and mixed solution leaves at $80\,\text{mL/s}.$
As a result, the amount of solution in the vat after $t$ seconds is 

$$
V(t)=6\,500+100t-80t=20(325+t)\,\text{mL}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the vat is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of sugar in the vat, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{20(325+t)}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{mL}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $80\,\text{mL/s},$ *sugar* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(80\,\frac{\text{mL}}{\text{s}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{20(325+t)}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{mL}}) \\  & =(80\,\frac{\cancel{\text{mL}}}{\text{s}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{20(325+t)}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\cancel{\text{mL}}}) \\  & =\frac{4Q}{325+t}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{s}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0-\frac{4Q}{325+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}=-\frac{4}{325+t}\,Q.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{4}{325+t} \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt}dt & =\int (-\frac{4}{325+t})\,dt \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \,dQ & =-4\int \frac{1}{325+t}\,dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =-4(\operatorname{ln}⁡|325+t|)+C \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|(325+t)^{-4}|+C \\ |Q| & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|(325+t)^{-4}|+C} \\ Q(t) & =\frac{A}{(325+t)^{4}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $A=\pm {e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the vat initially contains $300\,\text{g}$ of sugar. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=300,$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =300 \\ \frac{A}{(325+0)^{4}} & =300 \\ A & =300(325)^{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =\frac{300(325)^{4}}{(325+t)^{4}} \\  & =300{(\frac{325}{325+t})}^{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the vat begins to overflow. The vat has a capacity of $9\,500\,\text{mL},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=9\,500$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =9\,500 \\ 20(325+{t}_{o}) & =9\,500 \\ 325+{t}_{o} & =475 \\ {t}_{o} & =150\,\text{s}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the amount of sugar in the vat at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(150) & =300{(\frac{325}{325+150})}^{4} \\  & =300{(\frac{13}{19})}^{4} \\  & ≈65.75\,\text{g},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places.
